slides.heading: Welcome: Mandatory Reporting in Nevada
bullets: Who is a mandated reporter in Nevada
What abuse and neglect can look like
Who to report to, and how fast
How to respond to a disclosure and document it
slides.narration: Welcome to Nevada Mandatory Reporter Training. Thank you for taking the time to do this. The work you do every day puts you close to kids and families, and sometimes that means you will notice when something is wrong. This course will help you know what to do when that happens. We will cover who has to report under Nevada law, what abuse and neglect can look like, how quickly you need to act, and who you call. We will also talk about what to say if a child tells you something, and how to write it down the right way. At the end there is a short quiz. Let's get started.

slides.heading: You Are a Mandated Reporter
bullets: Nevada law, NRS 432B, names many child-serving professionals
Behavior analysts are required to follow it
Spectrum Squad policy: every staff member reports
RBTs, BCBAs and office staff are all included
slides.narration: Nevada's child protection law is found in N R S four three two B. It lists many kinds of professionals who must report suspected child abuse or neglect. These include people in health care, education, social work, and child care. Nevada's rules for behavior analysts also require them to follow these reporting laws. Here at Spectrum Squad, our policy is simple. If you work with our clients, you are a mandated reporter. That means BCBAs, RBTs, and office staff too. Even if you are brand new to health care, this duty is yours from your very first session.

slides.heading: Reasonable Cause, Not Proof
bullets: You report a reasonable belief, not a proven fact
You do not need to know who did it
You do not need to be sure
Investigating is the agency's job, not yours
slides.narration: A lot of people wait to report because they are not sure. Here is the good news. You do not need proof. The standard is reasonable cause to believe. That means if a reasonable person with your training would suspect abuse or neglect based on what you saw or heard, you report. You do not need to know who did it. You do not need to be certain it happened. The child welfare agency and law enforcement are trained to look into it. Your job is to pass along what you know, quickly and honestly. When in doubt, report.

slides.heading: Physical and Sexual Abuse
bullets: Unexplained bruises, burns, welts or patterned marks
Injuries that don't match the explanation given
Sexual knowledge or behavior unusual for the child's age
Pain, bleeding or injury in private areas
slides.narration: Let's look at the types of abuse, starting with physical and sexual abuse. Physical abuse is when someone causes a child injury on purpose. Watch for bruises in unusual places like the back, ears, or upper arms, burns, welts, or marks shaped like a hand, belt, or cord. Pay attention when the story does not match the injury. For example, a parent says a child fell off the couch, but the bruises are on both sides of the face. Sexual abuse includes any sexual contact with a child, and also exposing a child to sexual material. Signs can include sexual knowledge or behavior that is unusual for the child's age and development, or pain or injury in private areas, which you might notice while helping with toileting.

slides.heading: Emotional Abuse, Neglect, Exploitation
bullets: Constant threats, insults or extreme fear of a caregiver
Missing food, hygiene, medical care or supervision
Unsafe homes, such as exposed drugs or weapons
Using a child for sex, labor or money
slides.narration: Emotional abuse is a pattern of treating a child in a way that harms their mental health, like constant threats, screaming insults, or terrorizing them. A child who seems truly terrified of one caregiver is worth noticing. Neglect is the most commonly reported type. It means a child is not getting basic needs met, like enough food, clean clothes, needed medical care, or safe supervision. Imagine you arrive for a home session and a four-year-old is alone, with no adult in the house. That is a supervision concern. Unsafe homes count too, such as drugs or loaded guns within a child's reach. Exploitation means using a child for sex, labor, or someone else's financial gain.

slides.heading: When Signs Overlap With Autism
bullets: Self-injury, sensory needs and meltdowns can cause marks
Many clients can't tell you what happened
Don't explain injuries away or diagnose them yourself
Record facts: what, where, when, size, what was said
slides.narration: This part is especially important in our work. Some of our clients engage in self-injury, like head banging or biting, and that can leave marks. Some have sensory needs or toileting delays. Many of our kids cannot tell us what happened to them, which actually makes them more vulnerable to abuse, not less. So be careful about two mistakes. Do not assume every bruise is abuse, and do not explain an injury away just because the child has autism. Instead, stick to the facts. Write down what you saw, where it was on the body, about how big it was, when you noticed it, and anything anyone said about it. If you still have reasonable cause to believe abuse or neglect happened, you report.

slides.heading: Report Within 24 Hours
bullets: As soon as reasonably practicable
No later than 24 hours after you suspect
Immediate danger? Call 911 first
Don't wait for your next session or a team meeting
slides.narration: Now let's talk about timing. Nevada law says you must report as soon as reasonably practicable, and no later than twenty-four hours after you know or have reasonable cause to believe a child has been abused or neglected. That clock starts when you become suspicious, not when you finish your shift or when your supervisor gets back to you. Do not wait until your next session, your next team meeting, or until you collect more evidence. And if a child is in immediate danger right now, call nine one one first. Safety always comes before paperwork.

slides.heading: Who to Call
bullets: A child welfare agency or law enforcement
In Clark County: Department of Family Services
Other counties: the local child welfare agency
Hotline numbers are in the Spectrum Squad policy
slides.narration: Reports go to a child welfare agency or to a law enforcement agency. Here in Las Vegas and the rest of Clark County, the child welfare agency is the Clark County Department of Family Services, often called D F S. They run a hotline that is answered around the clock. If a family lives in another county, you report to the child welfare agency for that area, or to law enforcement. You can find the current hotline numbers in our Spectrum Squad reporting policy and posted in the clinic. When you call, have the child's name, age, address if you know it, and the facts you observed ready to share.

slides.heading: Your Duty Can't Be Handed Off
bullets: Telling your supervisor does not meet your duty
You must make sure the report is actually made
Still notify your BCBA or supervisor right away
Failing to report is a crime under Nevada law
slides.narration: Here is something that surprises many new staff. Telling your supervisor is not the same as making a report. The duty belongs to you personally. You cannot hand it off. The safest way to meet it is to make the call yourself. You should also let your BCBA or supervisor know right away so they can support you and the client's care. But if your supervisor says not to report, or says they will handle it, you still need to make sure a report is actually made within twenty-four hours. Under Nevada law, knowingly and willfully failing to report is a misdemeanor, and repeat violations can be charged more seriously.

slides.heading: Good Faith Protects You
bullets: Good-faith reporters are immune from civil and criminal liability
Protection applies even if abuse isn't confirmed
Your name is generally kept confidential
Spectrum Squad will never punish a good-faith report
slides.narration: Many people worry about getting in trouble if they are wrong. Nevada law protects you. If you make a report in good faith, meaning you honestly believed it was needed, you are protected from civil and criminal liability, even if the agency finds no abuse. The law also generally keeps the reporter's identity confidential. And at Spectrum Squad, you will never be punished for making a good-faith report. We would much rather you report and be wrong than stay quiet and be right. The only thing that is never okay is knowingly making a false report.

slides.heading: Responding to a Disclosure
bullets: Stay calm, listen, and believe the child
Don't interrogate or ask leading questions
Don't promise to keep it a secret
Don't investigate or confront the parent
slides.narration: Sometimes a child will tell you something directly. Let's say you are working with an eight-year-old client at school, and she quietly says her uncle hurts her at night. Stay calm. Listen. Tell her, thank you for telling me, and you did the right thing. Do not interrogate her or ask leading questions like, did he touch you here. Too many questions can upset the child and can hurt the investigation later. Do not promise to keep it a secret, because you will need to tell people who can help. Do not try to investigate, take photos of private areas, or confront the parent or caregiver. That could put the child in more danger. Just listen, keep the child safe, and report.

slides.heading: Documenting Objectively
bullets: Write the child's exact words in quotes
Describe what you saw, not what you think
Note date, time, place and who was present
Keep it in approved records, not texts or notes apps
slides.narration: After you report, write it down while it is fresh. Use the child's exact words, in quotes, as best you can remember them. Describe what you saw, not your opinion. For example, write, two round bruises, each about the size of a dime, on the left upper arm. Do not write, looks like the dad grabbed him. Include the date, the time, where you were, and who was there. Note when you made the report, who you spoke to, and any reference number they gave you. Keep all of this in our approved records system, never in personal texts or a notes app on your phone.

slides.heading: Adult Clients and Recap
bullets: Nevada also protects older and vulnerable adults
Use the same steps and timeline for adult clients
Reasonable cause, 24 hours, report it yourself
Now take the quiz: you need 80% to pass
slides.narration: One last note. Some of our clients are adults. Nevada has a separate law, N R S two hundred point five zero nine three, that covers abuse, neglect, and exploitation of older and vulnerable adults, with a similar twenty-four hour timeline. If you have concerns about an adult client, follow the same steps and talk with your supervisor about where to report. Let's recap. You are a mandated reporter. You need reasonable cause, not proof. Report to the child welfare agency or law enforcement as soon as you can, and no later than twenty-four hours. Call nine one one if a child is in danger. You personally must make sure the report is made, and also tell your supervisor. Good-faith reports are protected. Listen without interrogating, and document only the facts. Now it's time for the quiz. You need a score of eighty percent to pass. You've got this.

quiz.question: During a home session, you notice a bruise on a client's upper arm. The parent's explanation doesn't match the injury, but you aren't sure abuse happened. What should you do?
choices: Wait until you see more bruises so you have proof
Report it, because reasonable cause to believe is enough
Ask the parent more questions until you are sure
Do nothing, since the child cannot confirm what happened
quiz.explanation: Nevada requires a report when you have reasonable cause to believe abuse or neglect occurred. You do not need proof or certainty.

quiz.question: You become concerned about possible neglect on Monday at 4 p.m. What is the latest you can report under Nevada law?
choices: By the end of the week
At your next scheduled session with the client
After your supervisor reviews it at the monthly meeting
As soon as reasonably practicable, and no later than 4 p.m. Tuesday
quiz.explanation: Nevada requires a report as soon as reasonably practicable and no later than twenty-four hours after you suspect abuse or neglect.

quiz.question: An RBT tells her BCBA about a child's disclosure. The BCBA says, "I'll take care of it." Two days later, no report has been made. What went wrong?
choices: The RBT's duty could not be handed off; she needed to make sure a report was made within 24 hours
Nothing, because telling a supervisor meets the RBT's duty
The RBT should have confronted the parent first
The RBT should have waited for more evidence before telling anyone
quiz.explanation: Your duty to report is personal and cannot be delegated. You should notify your supervisor, but you must also make sure the report is actually made.

quiz.question: You arrive at a client's home in Las Vegas and find the four-year-old alone with no adult present. You can't reach anyone. What is the best first step?
choices: Leave and document it in tomorrow's session note
Text the parent and wait for a reply
Call 911, since the child may be in immediate danger
Start the session and mention it to the parent later
quiz.explanation: When a child may be in immediate danger, call 911 first. Safety comes before paperwork.

quiz.question: A client with autism who engages in head banging has a new bruise on his forehead. What is the best approach?
choices: Assume it is from self-injury and do not write anything down
Assume it is abuse and confront the caregiver
Ask the child yes-or-no questions until he answers
Document the facts objectively, and report if you have reasonable cause to believe abuse occurred
quiz.explanation: Some autism behaviors can cause injuries, so record facts carefully and avoid explaining injuries away. If reasonable cause remains, you report.

quiz.question: Your client lives in Clark County. Where should your report of suspected child abuse go?
choices: The client's school principal
The Clark County Department of Family Services or law enforcement
The client's insurance company
The BACB, the national certification board
quiz.explanation: Reports go to a child welfare agency or law enforcement. In Clark County, the child welfare agency is the Department of Family Services.

quiz.question: During a school session, a child quietly says, "My uncle hurts me at night." What is the best response?
choices: Stay calm, listen, thank her for telling you, and don't promise to keep it secret
Ask detailed questions like, "Did he touch you here?"
Promise you won't tell anyone so she keeps talking
Call the uncle to hear his side of the story
quiz.explanation: Listen calmly and supportively without interrogating or asking leading questions. Never promise secrecy, and never confront the alleged abuser.

quiz.question: Which session note is written most objectively?
choices: "Looks like Dad grabbed him again."
"Client is clearly being abused at home."
"Two round bruises, each about dime-sized, on left upper arm, noted at 3:15 p.m."
"Mom seems like a bad parent."
quiz.explanation: Objective documentation describes what you saw, with size, location and time, not opinions or conclusions.

quiz.question: An RBT made a report in good faith. The agency later found no abuse. What happens to the RBT?
choices: She can be sued by the family for damages
She will be written up by Spectrum Squad for being wrong
She loses her RBT credential
She is protected, because good-faith reporters are immune from liability
quiz.explanation: Nevada protects people who report in good faith from civil and criminal liability, even when abuse is not confirmed.

quiz.question: A BCBA serves an adult client and suspects the client is being financially exploited by a caregiver. What should she do?
choices: Nothing, because mandatory reporting only applies to children
Follow the same steps and timeline, and talk with her supervisor about where to report
Investigate the caregiver's bank records herself
Wait until the client's annual reassessment
quiz.explanation: Nevada has a separate law protecting older and vulnerable adults with a similar twenty-four hour timeline, so follow the same steps.
